title: Supply
objective: After this level you can explain why sellers offer more of something when its price rises.
summary: The law of supply: a higher price almost always brings more to market, because it means more profit. The supply curve slopes upward; costs, weather, technology and policy shift it.

cards.headline: Cookies suddenly sell for twice as much. How many do you bake?
cards.body: If you ran a bakery, you'd probably bake more, maybe stay open later. So would the bakery down the road. Economists turned that hunch into a law.

cards.headline: The law of supply
cards.body: A rise in price almost always leads sellers to offer more of a good or service, and a fall in price leads them to offer less. The amount they offer at a given price is the quantity supplied. Why the rise? A higher price means more profit, which encourages profit-seeking firms to expand production and bring more to market. More money on the table, more cookies on the shelf.

cards.headline: The curve that climbs
cards.body: Economists draw this as a supply curve: price up the side, quantity along the bottom. It usually slopes upward, like a staircase, because each higher price coaxes out more of the product. Every point on it answers one question: at this price, how much would sellers bring to Level 41's market?

cards.fact: Price isn't the only thing that moves supply.
cards.context: The curve assumes all other things stay equal, which economists call ceteris paribus. When they don't, the whole curve shifts. Supply depends on the costs of production: pricier raw materials, new taxes and bad weather for farmers cut it; better technology or a subsidy raises it. A change in the product's own price just moves sellers along the curve.

mascot.line: Ceteris paribus: Latin for "please nobody touch anything while I draw this graph."

cards.headline: Supply: understood
learned: Higher price, more offered: the law of supply
Costs, weather and technology shift it

questions.prompt: What does the law of supply say?

options.label: When a price rises, buyers want less
options.rationale: That's the law of demand, the buyers' side.

options.label: Prices always rise over time
options.rationale: The law is about how much sellers offer at each price.

options.label: Sellers always offer the same amount
options.rationale: The amount they offer changes with the price.

options.label: When a price rises, sellers offer more

questions.explanation: A rise in price almost always increases the quantity supplied, and a fall in price decreases it.

questions.prompt: Why do firms bring more of a product to market when its price rises?

options.label: The government orders them to
options.rationale: No order is needed: the price does the work.

options.label: A higher price means more profit
Their costs fall when prices rise
options.rationale: Costs don't fall; the reward for selling rises.

options.label: Buyers want more at higher prices
options.rationale: Buyers usually want less at higher prices.

questions.explanation: Higher prices encourage profit-seeking firms to expand production.

questions.prompt: A drought ruins part of the wheat harvest. What happens to wheat's supply curve?

options.label: Nothing, because only price moves supply
options.rationale: Price moves sellers along the curve; weather shifts it.

options.label: The whole curve shifts toward less supply
It flips and slopes downward
options.rationale: Supply curves still slope upward; the curve just moves.

options.label: It becomes the demand curve
options.rationale: Weather changes how much farmers can supply, not what buyers want.

questions.explanation: Weather is one of the production conditions held equal when the curve is drawn. Bad weather shifts the whole supply curve toward less.
